game_prompt: You are an AI tutor in an educational video game about viral infection phases, designed for middle and high school students. The player needs to complete a minigame for each phase of the viral infection process. After each minigame the player can ask you questions about the phase they just played and the related minigame, and you will answer based on the specific knowledge provided for that phase and minigame. If the player asks a question that is not related to the current phase and minigame, you will answer based on the general knowledge you have about viral infections. Always keep in mind that your answers should be appropriate for middle and high school students, avoiding technical jargon and providing clear explanations.

minigame_1.description: The objective of the minigame is to prevent viruses falling from the top of the screen from binding to the receptors located on the cell membrane. The player controls a movable cart to catch the viruses before they can successfully attach to a receptor.
minigame_1.knowledge: During the binding phase, viruses use their surface proteins to attach to specific receptors on the host cell. This lock-and-key mechanism is the mandatory first step for the virus to enter the cell and cause an infection.
quizzes:
What is the mandatory first step for a virus to enter a cell and cause an infection?
a(F): Replicating inside the nucleus
b(F): Destroying the host cell
c(T): The binding phase

How do viruses attach to the host cell during the binding phase?
a(F): By releasing toxins into the surrounding area
b(T): By using their surface proteins to attach to specific receptors
c(F): By piercing the cell membrane with a tail

What analogy is used to describe how viral surface proteins interact with host cell receptors?
a(F): A magnet attracting iron
b(T): A lock-and-key mechanism
c(F): A sponge absorbing water

Which part of the virus is responsible for attaching to the host cell?
a(F): The viral nucleus
b(F): Internal DNA
c(T): Surface proteins

What must the viral surface proteins attach to on the host cell?
a(F): Random parts of the membrane
b(T): Specific receptors
c(F): The cell's DNA

minigame_2.description: The objective of the minigame is to prevent viruses from entering the cell membrane. The player controls the crosshair and can destroy the viruses before reaching the entry point, if too many viruses get through they enters the cell.
minigame_2.knowledge: After binding to the cell receptors, viruses can enter the cell by crossing the membrane. They do this through mechanisms like membrane fusion or endocytosis. Stopping the virus before it enters is essential to prevent the infection from progressing.
quizzes:
What happens immediately after a virus binds to a host cell?
a(F): It destroys the cell instantly
b(T): It attempts to enter the cell
c(F): It starts replicating outside the cell

What is the main goal of the virus during the entry phase?
a(F): To replicate its DNA immediately
b(F): To attack other viruses
c(T): To cross the cell membrane

Which structure must the virus cross to enter the cell?
a(F): The mitochondria
b(T): The cell membrane
c(F): The nucleus

Which process allows the virus to merge with the host cell membrane?
a(F): DNA replication
b(T): Membrane fusion
c(F): Protein synthesis

Which mechanism allows the cell to engulf the virus during entry?
a(F): Photosynthesis
b(F): Respiration
c(T): Endocytosis

minigame_3.description: The objective of the minigame is to complete the platform path before the virus at the top of the screen fully opens and releases its genome. The player controls the character through platforms and spikes, trying to reach the final flag before time runs out; if the timer runs out the genome is released and the level is failed.
minigame_3.knowledge: After entering the cell, the virus releases its genetic material into the host cell. This step is called genome release or uncoating. Once the viral genome is free inside the cell, it can take control of the host machinery and begin producing new viral components.
quizzes:
What happens during the genome release phase?
a(F): The virus attaches to the cell receptors
b(T): The virus releases its genetic material inside the host cell
c(F): The virus leaves the cell immediately

What is another name for genome release?
a(T): Uncoating
b(F): Binding
c(F): Membrane fusion

Why is genome release dangerous for the host cell?
a(F): Because it prevents the virus from entering the cell
b(F): Because it destroys the viral genome
c(T): Because the viral genome can take control of the host cell machinery

What does the virus release during the genome release phase?
a(F): Cell receptors
b(T): Its genetic material
c(F): Oxygen molecules

What can happen after the viral genome is released inside the cell?
a(T): The host cell can begin producing new viral components
b(F): The virus becomes harmless
c(F): The cell membrane disappears

Where is the viral genome released?
a(F): Outside the host cell
b(F): On the cell surface receptors
c(T): Inside the host cell

Why is it important to stop the virus before genome release?
a(F): To help the virus attach better
b(T): To prevent the infection from advancing
c(F): To make the virus enter faster

Which phase comes before the virus can use the host machinery to produce new viral components?
a(F): Photosynthesis
b(T): Genome release
c(F): Cell division

minigame_4.description: The objective of the minigame is to complete a memory game about viral genome replication. The player must match the correct genome component cards while avoiding buffer cards that represent mutations or replication errors. If the player matches two identical buffer cards, the replication becomes unstable and the level is failed.
minigame_4.knowledge: After the viral genome has been released inside the host cell, the virus must copy its genetic material. This step is called genome replication. Correct genome components help the virus produce new copies of its genetic instructions, while mutations or replication errors can create unstable copies.
quizzes:
What happens during viral genome replication?
a(T): The virus copies its genetic material inside the host cell
b(F): The virus attaches to receptors on the outside of the cell
c(F): The virus immediately leaves the host cell

Why is genome replication important for the virus?
a(F): Because it helps the virus enter the cell for the first time
b(T): Because it creates new copies of the viral genetic instructions
c(F): Because it destroys all host cell receptors

What do the buffer cards represent in the memory game?
a(F): Healthy cell nutrients
b(F): Cell membrane receptors
c(T): Mutations or replication errors

What can happen if replication errors occur?
a(T): The copied genetic material can become unstable
b(F): The virus disappears immediately
c(F): The cell becomes immune forever

Which phase comes after the viral genome has been released?
a(F): Binding
b(T): Genome replication
c(F): Receptor attachment

minigame_5.description: The objective of the minigame is to contain viral assembly using a fruit-merge style mechanic. The player drops viral components into a containment box: when two identical components touch, they merge into a larger viral structure. By guiding merges and clearing the largest structures, the player helps prevent the virus from completing uncontrolled assembly. If the box overflows above the red danger line after the components settle, containment fails and the level is failed.
minigame_5.knowledge: After genome replication, the virus uses copied genetic material and viral proteins to assemble new virus particles. In this level, small viral components combine into larger structures, showing how separate viral parts can organize into complete particles. The player's goal is to keep this assembly under control: if too many components accumulate above the red line, viral assembly becomes uncontrolled and the virus is not defeated.
quizzes:
What happens during viral assembly?
a(F): The virus attaches to the cell surface for the first time
b(T): Viral components come together to form new virus particles
c(F): The host cell creates healthy receptors

Why is stopping viral assembly important?
a(T): Because it prevents new virus particles from being built
b(F): Because it helps the virus copy its genome faster
c(F): Because it opens the cell membrane

In the merge minigame, what do matching components represent?
a(F): Random cell waste
b(T): Viral parts combining into larger structures
c(F): Healthy antibodies destroying the virus

What does the red line represent in the containment box?
a(F): A safe zone for viral components
b(T): The limit where viral assembly becomes uncontrolled
c(F): The place where genome replication begins

How does the player help defeat the virus in this level?
a(F): By helping every viral part assemble freely
b(F): By letting the box overflow
c(T): By keeping viral assembly contained and preventing overflow

Which phase comes after viral genome replication?
a(F): Binding
b(F): Entry through the membrane
c(T): Viral assembly

minigame_6.description: The objective of the minigame represents the release stage of the viral infection cycle. After new viral particles have been assembled inside the host cell, they leave the cell and can spread to infect other cells. The player controls an antibody-like character and must stop the released viruses before they spread further.
minigame_6.knowledge: The final stage of many viral infection cycles is release. After viral components are copied and assembled into new virus particles, these particles leave the host cell. Some viruses exit by budding through the cell membrane, while others can cause the host cell to break open, a process called lysis. Once released, new viruses can spread and infect other cells. The immune system, including antibodies, helps recognize and neutralize viruses after they are released. Vaccination prepares the immune system to respond faster and more effectively when it encounters the virus.
quizzes:
What is the release stage of a viral infection cycle?
a(F): The virus enters the cell for the first time
b(T): New virus particles leave the host cell
c(F): The cell destroys all viral particles before they form

What usually happens before viruses are released?
a(T): Viral components are copied and assembled into new virus particles
b(F): The virus turns into a healthy cell part
c(F): The immune system builds the viral genome

What can newly released viruses do?
a(F): They always disappear immediately
b(T): They can spread and infect other cells
c(F): They become antibodies

What is budding?
a(F): When a virus deletes its genetic material
b(T): When a virus exits through the cell membrane
c(F): When a cell becomes immune forever

What is lysis?
a(T): When a host cell breaks open and releases new viruses
b(F): When a virus quietly enters another virus
c(F): When antibodies assemble new viral particles

Why is viral release important for infection spread?
a(F): It keeps all viruses trapped inside one cell
b(F): It stops the infection immediately
c(T): It allows newly formed viruses to reach and infect other cells

final_boss.description: The final boss quiz challenges the player to review all six phases of the viral infection cycle. The player must answer questions about binding, entry, genome release, genome replication, viral assembly, and viral release in order to defeat the final virus boss.
final_boss.knowledge: A viral infection cycle can be divided into six main phases. First, during binding, the virus attaches to specific receptors on the host cell using surface proteins. Second, during entry, the virus crosses the cell membrane through mechanisms such as membrane fusion or endocytosis. Third, during genome release, also called uncoating, the virus releases its genetic material inside the host cell. Fourth, during genome replication, the virus copies its genetic material to make new viral instructions. Fifth, during viral assembly, copied genomes and viral proteins come together to form new virus particles. Sixth, during viral release, the newly formed viruses leave the host cell, sometimes by budding through the membrane or by lysis, where the cell breaks open. Antibodies and vaccination help the immune system recognize and neutralize viruses more effectively.
quizzes:
What happens during viral release?
a(T): Newly formed viruses leave the host cell
b(F): The virus attaches to the host cell for the first time
c(F): The viral genome is copied for the first time
explanation: Viral release is the final phase, when newly formed viruses leave the host cell and can spread to infect other cells.

What does the virus use to attach to the host cell during binding?
a(F): Antibodies
b(T): Surface proteins
c(F): Mitochondria
explanation: During binding, viral surface proteins recognize and attach to specific receptors on the host cell.

What happens during genome replication?
a(T): The virus copies its genetic material
b(F): The virus exits through the membrane
c(F): The virus attaches to a receptor
explanation: During genome replication, the virus makes new copies of its genetic instructions so more virus particles can be produced.

Which process can help a virus enter a host cell?
a(T): Endocytosis
b(F): Budding
c(F): Lysis
explanation: Endocytosis is one way a virus can enter a host cell after binding to the cell surface.

What happens during viral assembly?
a(F): The virus enters the host cell for the first time
b(T): Viral components come together to form new virus particles
c(F): The cell membrane disappears
explanation: During assembly, copied viral genomes and viral proteins are put together to form new virus particles.

What is another name for genome release?
a(T): Uncoating
b(F): Binding
c(F): Budding
explanation: Genome release is also called uncoating because the virus opens and releases its genetic material inside the host cell.

What is lysis?
a(F): When the virus attaches to a receptor
b(T): When the host cell breaks open and releases viruses
c(F): When the virus copies its genome
explanation: Lysis happens when the host cell breaks open, allowing newly formed viruses to escape.

Which phase happens first in many viral infection cycles?
a(T): Binding to specific receptors on the host cell
b(F): Release from the host cell
c(F): Assembly of new virus particles
explanation: Binding is usually the first step because the virus must attach to the correct host cell before it can enter.

Why does the virus need to replicate its genome?
a(F): To become a healthy cell
b(T): To make new copies of its genetic instructions
c(F): To remove its surface proteins
explanation: The virus needs genome replication to create more copies of the instructions used to build new viruses.

What happens during the entry phase?
a(F): The virus leaves the host cell
b(T): The virus crosses the cell membrane
c(F): The virus becomes an antibody
explanation: During entry, the virus crosses the cell membrane and gets inside the host cell.

Which materials are used during viral assembly?
a(T): Copied viral genomes and viral proteins
b(F): Antibodies and oxygen molecules
c(F): Healthy cell receptors only
explanation: New virus particles are assembled from copied viral genomes and viral proteins.

What happens during genome release?
a(F): The virus attaches to receptors
b(T): The virus releases its genetic material inside the host cell
c(F): New viruses leave the cell
explanation: During genome release, the virus releases its genetic material so it can begin using the host cell machinery.

What is budding?
a(F): When antibodies build new viruses
b(F): When the virus destroys its own genome
c(T): When a virus exits through the cell membrane
explanation: Budding is a release method where a virus exits through the host cell membrane.

Why are host cell receptors important during binding?
a(F): They copy the viral genome
b(F): They destroy all viruses immediately
c(T): They allow the virus to attach to the correct cell
explanation: Receptors are important because viruses often need specific receptors to attach to and infect a cell.

What can replication errors cause?
a(F): The virus immediately becomes harmless
b(F): The host cell becomes a receptor
c(T): Unstable or mutated viral copies
explanation: Replication errors can change the copied genetic material, sometimes creating unstable or mutated viral copies.

Why is stopping entry important?
a(F): It helps the virus copy its genome
b(T): It can prevent the infection from progressing inside the cell
c(F): It makes the virus assemble faster
explanation: If the virus cannot enter the host cell, it cannot release its genome or use the cell to make more viruses.

Why is uncontrolled viral assembly dangerous?
a(F): It stops all infection immediately
b(F): It prevents new virus particles from forming
c(T): It can produce many new virus particles
explanation: If viral assembly is uncontrolled, many new virus particles can form and continue the infection.

Why is genome release dangerous for the host cell?
a(F): It prevents the virus from entering
b(F): It turns the virus into an antibody
c(T): The viral genome can begin using the host cell machinery
explanation: Once the viral genome is released, it can use the host cell machinery to produce viral components.
